analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the 2017 tax law's individual tax cuts, including lower rates, a doubled estate tax exemption, and the pass-through business deduction.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 220-191 on September 28, 2018, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 Republican tax law set most of its individual tax provisions to expire after 2025. This bill would write them into permanent law: the lower individual rates, the bigger standard deduction and child tax credit, the 20% deduction for pass-through business income, the doubled estate tax exemption, and higher alternative minimum tax exemptions. It would also permanently lock in the law's tax increases on some taxpayers, like the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes and the repeal of personal exemptions. The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote; the Senate Finance Committee never acted.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income taxpayers gain the most: the doubled estate tax exemption applies only to estates worth over roughly $10 million per person, and the permanent 20% deduction on pass-through business income flows mainly to owners of law firms, real estate partnerships, and other businesses taxed on individual returns. Ordinary working families would also keep the lower rates, a roughly doubled standard deduction ($12,000 single, $18,000 head of household), and a $2,000 child tax credit that they got under the 2017 law, which without this bill shrinks after 2025.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large estates, business owners, higher earners

how_it_helps.text: Permanently keeps the 2017 law's lower individual income tax rates, including the drop in the top rate from 39.6% to 37% [S2][S4].

Makes permanent the increased standard deduction — $12,000 for single filers and $18,000 for heads of household under this bill — which simplifies filing and cuts taxes for most taxpayers who no longer itemize [S4].
Makes permanent the doubled child tax credit of $2,000 per child, with up to $1,400 of it refundable for families who owe little or no income tax [S4].
Permanently allows the 20% deduction for qualified business income of pass-through entities such as sole proprietorships, partnerships, and S corporations [S2][S4].
Permanently sets the estate and gift tax exemption at $10 million per person (adjusted for inflation), removing the estate tax for all but the largest estates [S4].
Extends the 7.5% income threshold for deducting medical expenses through 2020, helping families with large out-of-pocket medical bills [S2][S4].
Permanently keeps student loans discharged because of the borrower's death or disability out of taxable income [S4].

analysis.who_pays: No provisions offset the cost, so future taxpayers bear it through larger deficits. Taxpayers who itemize in high-tax states keep paying the permanently capped $10,000 deduction on state and local taxes, and homeowners with large mortgages keep the permanent cap on deductible mortgage interest. The lowest-income families get little from the child tax credit, whose refundable portion stops at $1,400 and requires at least $2,500 of earned income.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes the $10,000 cap on state and local tax deductions permanent, locking in a tax increase for many homeowners in higher-tax states [S4].
It makes permanent the repeal of the personal exemption, a change that raises taxes for larger families who itemize [S2][S4].
The permanently doubled estate tax exemption is worth nothing to ordinary estates and only reduces taxes on estates over roughly $10 million per person [S4].
The refundable child tax credit is capped at $1,400 per child and requires $2,500 of earned income, so the lowest-earning families receive far less than the headline $2,000 [S4].
It permanently limits mortgage interest deductions to $750,000 of debt ($1 million for loans taken before December 2017) and restricts casualty-loss deductions to federally declared disasters [S4].

Nothing in the bill pays for the cost; all 184 House Democrats who voted supported a motion to attach a title aimed at protecting the Medicare and Social Security trust funds, reflecting concern that the deficit-financed tax cuts would drain those trust funds [S6][S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Working and middle-income families would keep a genuine tax cut — lower rates, a bigger standard deduction, and a larger child credit — that is currently scheduled to expire after 2025. But the design is skewed: the provisions worth the most per taxpayer, the doubled estate exemption and the pass-through deduction, concentrate their value on very wealthy estates and business owners, and nothing offsets the cost, which would add hundreds of billions to deficits over the decade. A bill designed to help ordinary families could have made the middle-class provisions permanent without locking in the estate tax doubling and pass-through break.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 220-191 on September 28, 2018, but the Senate referred it to its Finance Committee, which never acted before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Rodney Davis introduced the bill on September 10, 2018, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee [S1][S6].
The Ways and Means Committee ordered it reported 21-15 on September 13 and formally reported it amended on September 24 [S6].
The House passed it on September 28 by 220-191: 217 of 236 Republicans voted yes, while only 3 of 193 Democrats did [S8].

Rep. John Larson of Connecticut moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions to add a title called the Protect Medicare and Social Security Trust Funds Act; the motion failed 184-226, with all voting Republicans opposed and all voting Democrats in favor [S6][S7].
The Senate received the bill on October 1, 2018, read it twice, and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it sat with no vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Deficit hawks and defenders of the estate tax were better off, because the bill never became law and the deficit-financed provisions — including the permanent estate tax doubling and the top-rate cut — were not locked in. Large estates and pass-through business owners lost the chance at permanence, though the 2017 law's cuts to ordinary taxpayers were also left to expire.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Deficit hawks and estate tax defenders

industries.note: The bill permanently sets the estate and gift tax exemption at $10 million per person, eliminating the estate tax for all but the wealthiest families. Because it adds to deficits without offsets, the gain to these heirs comes at other taxpayers' expense.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (partnerships, law firms, real estate holdings)
industries.note: It permanently allows the 20% deduction on qualified business income, which disproportionately benefits owners of high-earning pass-through businesses. The permanent cost flows into federal deficits rather than any offset.
The bill makes the $10,000 cap on state and local tax deductions permanent, keeping a tax increase in place for high-income homeowners in states with high income or property taxes.
